fields.features_heading: What an Esthetician Intake Form Should Collect
fields.features_subheading: The questions an esthetician reads before a first facial, with every answer filed under the client's name.
fields.feature_1:
Skin concerns in the client's own words

Ask the client to pick a skin type, then describe the main concern in a sentence. The esthetician reads dry patches on the chin since October, not a single box ticked on a list.
fields.feature_2:
Products used morning and night

Give cleanser, serum, moisturizer, and sunscreen their own fields, and ask for the morning and evening routines separately. A retinol used only at night then shows up on the record.
fields.feature_3:
Allergies as a question nobody can skip

Make allergies a required yes or no, with a text box that opens on yes. Nobody can skip past it, and a blank field never reaches the esthetician looking like no allergies at all.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders until the form is finished

The app emails the intake link with the booking confirmation, then sends one reminder the day before if the form is still open. The front desk sees who has not finished yet.
fields.feature_5:
Photo permission and a signature at the end

Ask on their own whether progress photos may be taken and whether they may be posted. The client signs at the end to confirm the answers, and the date is saved next to the signature.
fields.feature_6:
Code your developer can take over

Export the full source to a GitHub repository on paid plans when intake belongs inside the studio's own booking site. A developer can host it anywhere and keep building on it.

fields.usecase_heading: How Spas and Studios Use Intake Answers
fields.tab_content_1:
Skin notes on Wren's screen the night before

Thistle Skin Studio sends the intake link with every first-facial booking. Lena Cho answers the day she books, noting combination skin and a fragrance allergy. The evening before, esthetician Wren Ito gets an email with those answers for the 10:00 facial. They stay on Lena's profile for later visits.
fields.tab_content_2:
A returning client changes one line, not the whole form

At Birchwood Day Spa, a returning client opens the intake with last visit's answers filled in. Maya Ferris last answered on March 4. She adds a vitamin C serum to her mornings and submits, and the front desk sees 1 change since March 4 on her record. An intake older than 12 months opens blank.
fields.tab_content_3:
Any yes in the health history waits for the nurse

Calla Med Spa runs one intake form for every service it books. A yes to any question in the health history section puts the booking on hold until nurse practitioner Bea Marsh reviews the record. Of today's 4 bookings, 2 are on hold, and the front desk can see which ones.
fields.tab_content_4:
Three photos ahead of every video consult

Ivy Rowe runs Fern Mobile Facials alone and offers a free 15-minute video consult before a first visit. The consult form asks for three daylight photos, front and both sides, plus a top concern. Elise Dunn picks uneven tone and sends her photos on Sunday. Ivy reads them before their Monday call at 6:30 pm.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Esthetician Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps that turn your services and questions into a working esthetician intake form, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List every service the form covers
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down each service the intake has to cover before you draft a question: facials, peels, waxing, and lash work. A question that matters for one service can then sit behind that choice, and a facial client never scrolls past lash questions.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Sit down with whoever does the treatments and ask which answers they need before a first appointment. Make those required. Anything they would only read out of interest becomes optional, which keeps a first-visit form short enough to finish on a phone.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Mark which answers the front desk needs for booking and which belong to the treating esthetician alone. Note it next to each section before you build. The access rules then go into your first prompt instead of being patched in later.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Put the services and who sees which answers into a plain-English prompt. Emergent builds the form with a record for each client and a database behind it. To move a question or add a service later, describe the change in a new prompt.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Connect it to your booking tool
fields.howto_step_5_des: If bookings live in another tool, the app can connect to it through that tool's API. The intake link then goes out with each confirmation, and every set of answers attaches to the appointment it belongs to, not to a loose email thread.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test it as a new and a returning client
fields.howto_step_6_des: Fill the form out yourself twice: once as a first-time facial client and once as a returning one. Check that each answer lands on the right record, that the reminder email arrives, and that a returning client sees last visit's answers.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share the link before the first visit
fields.howto_step_7_des: Put the link in the booking confirmation and on the studio's website. Clients who finish at home arrive with nothing left to fill out, and the esthetician starts the appointment having read every answer the night before.

faq_plan.q: What is an esthetician intake form?
faq_plan.a: An esthetician intake form is the questionnaire a client fills out before a skin treatment. It collects contact details, skin type, the products the client uses, any allergies, and what they want from the visit. The esthetician reads it before the appointment starts.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an esthetician intake form?
faq_plan.a: Tell Emergent's AI form builder which services you offer and which questions each one needs, in plain English. Emergent builds the form and the database that holds every answer from that prompt. Fill it out once as a new client before the link goes into your booking confirmations.

faq_plan.q: What questions go on an esthetician client intake form?
faq_plan.a: Start with contact details and date of birth. The skin questions come next: type, main concern, current products, and allergies. Add past professional treatments with rough dates and a free-text line for anything else. Emergent puts no cap on how many clients can fill it out.

faq_plan.q: Should a facial intake form include a signature?
faq_plan.a: Yes. End a facial intake form with a signature where the client confirms the answers are accurate and agrees to tell you if anything changes. Keep consent for a specific procedure on its own document, such as a permanent makeup consent form. Each document is then signed and updated on its own.

faq_plan.q: How is a medical spa client intake form different from a day spa form?
faq_plan.a: Build it with one extra section: a health history that a licensed provider reviews before treatment, on top of the skin and product questions a day spa form asks. Ask your medical director which questions that section holds, and send its answers to the provider, not the front desk.

faq_plan.q: When should a client fill out a spa consultation form?
faq_plan.a: Have the client fill it out when they book, or at least a day before the first appointment. At home they can read the labels on their products instead of guessing at the front desk. Keep a paper or tablet copy of the spa consultation form for walk-ins.

faq_plan.q: Can clients fill out an esthetician intake form on their phone?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The form Emergent builds opens from a link, and a client can answer and sign on a phone at home or in the waiting room. Use pickers for skin type and concerns, and nobody has to type long answers on a small screen. The same phone-first layout suits a tattoo consent form signed before a session.

faq_plan.q: How do I get clients to finish a spa intake form before the appointment?
faq_plan.a: Send the spa intake form with the booking confirmation and say how long it takes. Aim for about 5 minutes on a first visit by making only the must-know questions required. Clients who still have not finished can complete it at check-in on a tablet at the front desk.

faq_plan.q: Where should an esthetician keep completed client intake forms?
faq_plan.a: Keep them in one place tied to each client, not in a binder or a shared inbox, and limit who can open the health answers. With Emergent, every submitted form saves to a database you own, filed under the client's name.

faq_plan.q: Can one esthetician intake form cover facials, peels, and lash services?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Put a service picker at the top and show each service's questions only when it is chosen. A lash client never sees the peel questions. Contact details and allergies sit in a shared section, like a general intake form, that every client answers once.

plan.angle: The top 10 is spa pages, PDF forms, a Reddit thread, Etsy and three template builders, and every one stops at a sheet the client fills once on a clipboard. This page names what an esthetician intake form should collect and shows the form working in four real settings: a first facial where the answers reach the esthetician the night before, a returning client confirming only what changed, a med spa holding any yes in the health history for a nurse practitioner, and a solo esthetician taking photos before a video consult. Everything is framed as what the business collects and who sees it, never as skin or medical advice.
